They were doing their business in a secluded place, away from the camp. They were both married men and they were doing this business together because they were friends. One was from the Wolf clan, the other from the Turtle clan. They were doing their business by moonlight. They were both naked to the waist. The warrior had a belted sword on his hips, a knife on his left hip, a tomahawk on his right hip, and a bag of flint and steel on his back. The magic man had a bag of magic fruits, one of which was the "Old Woman" fruit, which could make the eater invisible for a night and day.The business the two men were doing was burning sweet grass. The warrior was grinding the sweet grass with a mortar and pestle while the magic man was holding a pipe. When the grass was burned, the warrior inhaled the smoke while the magic man fanned the embers. Then they reversed positions.
The warrior said to the magic man, "I am the warrior, you are the magic man. I put you down and I raise you up." The magic man said, "I am the magic man, you are the warrior. I make you dance and I make you sweat." Then they laughed.
The warrior said, "I will go to the camp and tell them I have been doing secret business with you." The magic man said, "I will go to the camp and tell them I have been doing secret business with you." But when they went to the camp the warriors did not make fun of them or ask them any questions, because they knew that they had been doing secret business.

...a Canadian First Nations community in Ontario, were fishing on Lake Huron in November 1982 when they were attacked by three men from another community, resulting in the deaths of two fisherman and one attacker. It led to a trial and conviction of the three attackers, which was appealed on the grounds of racial discrimination. The case, known as "The Egulac Case", was heard by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1989. It resulted in a ruling that the trial judge had not adequately explained the concept of "native" in the context of the Canadian constitution, and that the accused were not "everyday" Canadians. The case paved the way for the recognition of Aboriginal custom adopting and the Aboriginal rights movement.

The incident
On November 12, 1982, two men, 35-year-old William Mukashi and 22-year-old James Wemigabin, two members of the Egulac First Nation, were fishing in a boat on Lake Huron near the North Channel Marine Railway Bridge, when they were attacked by three men in a second boat. The attackers, members of the nearby Fort William First Nation, were 25-year-old Christopher Augustine, 28-year-old Joseph Augustine (Chris' brother), and 22-year-old Raymond O'Brien. The Egulac men were anchored for the night and were awakened by the approach of the Augustine brothers' boat. Mukashi went to the water's edge to meet the incoming boat while Wemigabin remained in the boat with the two other men from the community who had been with them (Peter St. Amand and Richard Wetatish) and their 11-year-old cousin. As Mukashi approached the Augustine boat, he was clubbed in the head and then dragged into the Augustine boat.

Two men were arrested for the crime. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: One of the two men, known as John R. aka "Johnny", was sentenced to prison for ten years. He was released after serving eight. The other man, known as William, was sentenced to prison for five years. He was released after serving three. Later, both men were sued for damages by the relatives of the kidnapped woman. They were awarded $6,500 in damages.Subsequently, the two men were found to be innocent of the crime. They were released from prison and compensated for their wrongful conviction.The story is told in "The Night Two Men from Egulac Came to Camp" from the book Indian Camp Songs and Stories by Francis Hewitt Pockridge. It is also told in William Wayer's book Native American Stories.

Whelan of the Ontario Provincial Police. The men were from the reserve at Ohsweken, near Brantford, Ontario, and were camping at a site on Pine Tree Hill on the outskirts of Brantford. Then it was market night and the people from the pueblo came down to the river, kanging (the hide coverings) and making ready to trade. News! A long time ago! One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the water rose, the tide came in, and the two men were left on an island of grass. Their fire went out, and they could not find another match. One of the men took off his belt and wrapped it around the other man's neck, and they lay down on the grass and waited for morning. But in the night the tide went out, and the current dragged one of the men out to the sea. The other man waited until dawn, then he went home and told the people on the reserve that his brother had been taken by the water-spirit. And that is why, to this day, the natives of Egulac never go out to hunt seals without taking a match with them. (From "River Under the Moon", 1981)  This is a story by Northwest Coast artist and writer Mungo Martin. It is one of a series of stories that were inspired by the art of the Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast of North America.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then it was market night and the town was all lit up. Suddenly, the people near the shore saw a light out on the water and then they saw two forms walking on the water, coming near to the shore. Some people thought they were apparitions and others said they were the Mollemen, but in any case they went to the mission to report what they had seen.

The old chief was there and he said he would go and see for himself. He put on his cloak and went out on the road by the river, but he never came back. For three days the people waited and then they went to look for him along the river, but he was not there. Then they went to look for the two young men who had gone out to hunt seals, but they were not there either. They went to the place where the old chief had gone and there were two canoes, one larger than the other. In the larger canoe was the old chief, and in the other was a young man who was alive but who could not speak.

The people were amazed and did not know what to think. Then the Mollemen came and took the young man away and said he would be all right. Afterward the old chief's spirit came to the people and told them that he had gone to help his son and that he was now dead. He said that the Mollemen had come to take him away because he had helped the people so often that they wanted to take him away from them. He said that the young man would be all right, that he would live, but that he would never speak again. He said that the Mollemen were very powerful and that they could make a man alive again, but that they would never speak.

Then he said that he was going to live with the Mollemen and that he would never come back

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the wind rose, and the water began to chill. One of the men took off his mask, and soon after that, the other one did the same. Just then a canoe came up and two men from the village of Wickanish pulled in. "What happened?" one of them asked. "We thought we heard voices," said the other. The two men from Egulac said nothing for a long time. Then one of them spoke. "Some people," he said, "think that the world was made in six days. I used to think that too, but now I'm not so sure." He pointed towards the river. "Look at that," he said. "The world didn't just happen. It evolved. It has been evolving for a long, long time, and it will keep on evolving."  from "The Two Young Men from Egulac" by Richard Wagamese.

The young men never went out again, and soon afterwards, two canoes came up, and took them away. They went up the river to the big town, and there they were put among the slaves.  This is the tale of the Egulac boys who went up the river to make war on the people.


== Information ==
This is a tale from the collection of the Smithsonian Institution, and is one of the stories told by the Kwakiutl people. The story is told in the words of the storyteller, as recorded by Edward A. Hayes in 1959. The story is a cautionary tale, warning of the dangers of going on a war-party.

The people jumped up and cried. He was dead.

He drew apart the hair on his head, and said: "If you wish to count me as one, then give me one arrow; if you do not count me as one, then give me two arrows." They counted him as one, and gave him one arrow. They counted the other young man as one, and gave him two arrows. That night they reached the village. The people came down to the water and they began to fight, and many were killed. But presently the young men who had gone down to the river to hunt seals came back, and they heard the noise of war-cries, and they knew that the enemy was there. And they took their wives and their dependents to the church, and shut the door. And they armed themselves, and went out to fight. And they fought all day long, and many were killed, and at night they counted the bodies. And there were five men killed.
